vision.title: The Adventure Begins
vision.premise: Keen leaves home for Crystal Cove wearing borrowed confidence and his father’s empty wristbands; a storm strips away the performance until he must choose real courage to save Squeaky and arrive not as a boy who “has this,” but as a bear who knows he is held by family, memory, and the new circle waiting for him.
vision.dramaticQuestion: When Keen’s brave face is taken apart by distance, weather, and someone else’s need, can he stop pretending he is fearless and let true courage carry him through?
vision.theme: Courage is not being alone without fear; courage is feeling the fear, feeling who loves you, and acting anyway.
vision.externalJourney: Keen departs the pier, meets Squeaky, gets caught in a storm, loses his map and boat, follows Squeaky into rough water, frees her from the drift net, is rescued by her, and reaches Crystal Cove where the bears welcome him and his aquamarine crystal settles into his father’s wristbands.
vision.internalJourney: Keen begins by performing certainty for his Mum and for himself: “I’ve got this, Mum.” The water reveals that confidence as borrowed. He becomes lost, afraid, and then faced with Squeaky’s need. His turn is not a power-up; it is surrender into sincerity. The wristbands glow when his father’s love, his Mum’s promise, and Keen’s own choice align. By the end, “Hi… I’m Keen” lands as a real introduction, not a brave mask.
vision.relationshipChanges: The heart relationship is Keen and his Mum: she lets him go without letting the ache become a cage, and he carries her love into the unknown. Aida becomes the bridge between home and Cove, witnessing what Mum cannot see and sending reassurance back. Keen and Squeaky begin as playful strangers and become rescue partners. Fuzzby and Zenny carry the comic relationship spine: his frantic self-importance needs her clean truth, and her restraint lets his big feeling stay lovable rather than noisy. The bears move from distant witnesses to chosen family.
vision.emotionalCurve: The episode opens in play: pollen, bravado, dry affection. It quietly deepens through Aida’s bowl and Mum’s held pride. The goodbye is the first ache, warmed by Keen’s wobble. The open water begins as adventure, then tightens into lostness. The shore scenes widen the fear into communal concern. The nadir is underwater: Keen’s strength fading, Squeaky trapped, the wristbands beginning to glow. The climax releases into action and terror together, then relief arrives wet, breathless, and laughing. The ending warms into belonging but keeps the trace of cost through Mum’s absence and the wristbands’ meaning.
vision.comedyCurve: Comedy starts high and behavioural with Fuzzby converting every failure into proof of mastery, while Zenny’s flat precision punctures him without cruelty. It returns as emergency comedy when Fuzzby is too panicked to be useful until Zenny supplies the truth. After the rescue, comedy becomes release: Keen laughs out terror with “Best… ride… ever!”, Fuzzby instantly mythologizes him, and the honey question turns welcome into friendship appetite. The final laugh is not random; it proves Fuzzby has accepted Keen fully and excessively, exactly as himself.
vision.setupPayoffMap: Fuzzby’s “Nailed it” and “Buzz Crash!!” set up the episode’s false-bravado language, paid off by Keen’s “Still got it!” as the same cover over a much deeper goodbye. The pollen moustache/goatee escalates Fuzzby’s need to look official, paid off when real emergency makes him emotionally sincere but verbally jammed. Aida’s rose-quartz bowl vision sets her as witness-from-a-distance, paid off when she sees Keen in the storm and sends Squeaky home with news for Mum. Mum’s vacant wristbands are planted as grief and protection, paid off underwater when they glow from within and become the vessel for Keen’s aquamarine crystal. Squeaky’s playful arrival at the pier sets trust, paid off when Keen follows her into rough water and later when she saves him. The map gag — “one of the directions” — plants that Keen’s confidence depends on appearing oriented, paid off when the storm takes the map and forces inner orientation. The shore beacon sets communal love across distance, paid off by Keen riding toward the glowing shore.
vision.visualMotifs: Empty wristbands becoming meaningful light. Water as the distance between being protected and choosing for yourself. The boat shrinking against open water. Pollen bravado versus storm truth. Circles: Aida’s bowl, the bears’ gathering circle, the warm circle around Keen on the sand. Light crossing weather: rose-quartz signal, combined beacon, aquamarine settling into family memory. Held paws: Mum placing the wristbands, Keen gripping the net, the group enclosing him without crowding him.
vision.sonicMotifs: Fuzzby’s busy chant and crash rhythm establish comic motion before the storm interrupts it. The crystal bowl note gives way to distant wind, linking Aida’s knowing to the weather coming. Thunder cuts through comedy as the tonal turn. Keen’s repeated “I’ve got this…” shifts from performance to self-steadying. The bears’ joined Crystal Call becomes a signal across fear rather than a solution. The aquamarine note should resolve only after Keen has already acted with sincerity. Squeaky’s chatter begins playful and becomes relational — not language, but trust.
vision.climax: Underwater, Keen reaches Squeaky, the net resists, the current shoves them, and his performed confidence finally has no audience left. The father’s wristbands glow from within; on shore, Aida names the truth: “He’s not alone.” Keen braces, pulls through the glow, tears the net free, and is thrown away by the wave. The rescue completes not because he becomes fearless, but because he acted while afraid — and Squeaky then catches him in return.
vision.resolution: Keen arrives in the shallows, releases the terror as laughter, and meets the Crystal Bears from a place of earned openness. Aida names the courage he has already lived; the aquamarine light appears, splits, and settles into the wristbands, turning inherited love into Keen’s own crystal strength. The final beach walk lets relief breathe through Fuzzby’s honey-friendship obsession, ending with laughter and belonging rather than a lecture.
vision.intendedFinalFeeling: Warm, proud, and a little tender: the child should feel the thrill of a storm ride and a new friendship; the adult should feel the ache of a parent letting go and the comfort of love that travels farther than the dock. The ending should not feel like the fear vanished — it should feel like Keen now knows what to do with it.

treatments.name: Treatment 1 — Mum’s Hands Let Go Before Her Heart Does
treatments.audienceExperience: The audience experiences the scene as a parent-sized act of courage disguised as a child’s departure. Children read the packing, the wobble, the dolphin, and the boat adventure; adults feel the harder story underneath: Mum choosing not to hold Keen back. The scene should make viewers smile at Keen’s proud little performance, then breathe in when the vacant wristbands enter, then release on the wobble and Squeaky’s arrival.
treatments.emotionalPointOfView: Mum governs the emotional point of view. Keen is leaving, but the scene is about the bear who stays behind and must make her paws open. Her want is to keep him safe by checking, fussing, and delaying. Her need is to trust that love can travel farther than her arms. Keen’s want is to prove he is ready; his need is to receive the promise without turning it into a performance.
treatments.comicOrDramaticMechanism: The dramatic mechanism is restraint under pressure: Mum keeps making ordinary practical gestures because the true feeling is too large to name. The comic release is hiding failure: Keen’s wobble becomes funny because he covers it with “Still got it!” as if the boat had witnessed greatness. Squeaky adds misunderstanding as warmth, not gag machinery: Keen answers dolphin chatter as if he has made a perfectly normal new friend.
treatments.characterPerformanceStrategy: Mum’s performance lives in interrupted touch: a paw that straightens an already-straight bundle, a breath that nearly becomes a sob but turns into a smile, the careful placement of the wristbands as if they are both precious and heavy. She never collapses into sentiment; her bravery is composure with leaks. Keen begins over-bright and busy, packing to avoid feeling watched. At the wristbands, his forward energy stops; his paws receive before his face knows what to do. His small courage tell appears before push-off: swallow, ears flatten for a breath, shoulders square, chin lifts. After the wobble, he re-inflates too fast, proving the mask is still there but softer. Squeaky’s arrival lets his real curiosity break through the goodbye ache.
treatments.visualGrammar: The scene is visually built around hands, distance, and soft morning air. The pier is not a postcard; it is a threshold. Frames compress around paws, wristbands, cheek, rope fibres, and the tiny spaces between Mum and Keen, then gradually allow more water into the image as leaving becomes irreversible. The gold wristbands remain vacant: worn, meaningful, unlit, carrying memory rather than magic. Warm morning light holds, but the water beyond has a faint cooler pull, hinting at the episode’s coming weather without stealing the goodbye.
treatments.cameraCharacterRelationship: The camera behaves like someone trusted inside the family’s personal space, but it never intrudes on Mum’s private breaking point. It stays close enough to feel her restraint in the paws, then lets Keen drift out of that closeness. When he pushes off, the camera does not lock itself safely to the dock; it briefly commits to the unstable boat experience, then rediscovers Mum as the remaining still point. No character owns a permanent screen side; geography is held by the dock, boat, ropes, and widening strip of water between them.
treatments.movementVersusStillness: Mum becomes stiller as the stakes grow, while Keen gets busier until the wristbands stop him. The scene’s movement is emotional subtraction: fewer fussing gestures, fewer excuses to touch, more space. The boat wobble breaks the restraint with a burst of physical comedy: Keen’s body overcorrects, paws windmill, balance returns by accident, pride arrives by choice. Squeaky’s splash introduces a new kind of motion — not escape from Mum, but invitation forward.
treatments.depthAndEnvironment: Depth carries the scene’s heart. Early, the pier environment wraps them: ropes, posts, bundles, boat edge, all close and protective. After the wristbands, the water gains depth behind Keen, and Mum’s world begins to recede. The closing geography should let even a young child understand: Mum on dock, Keen in boat, Squeaky beside him, open water ahead. The environment participates quietly: pier ropes stir during the father mention, the boat nudges the dock when neither of them can quite move, ripples widen after push-off.
treatments.rhythmAndEscalation: The rhythm starts practical and gently quick — checking, answering, packing. It slows around “big step,” then nearly stills when the wristbands appear. The promise is the emotional crest, but not the scene’s end; the scene must release into awkward action before it becomes too solemn. Escalation moves from Mum’s small delay tactics, to the irreplaceable gift, to the irreversible push-off, to the comic wobble, to the delighted interruption of Squeaky. The last feeling is nervous forward motion, not a sealed goodbye.
treatments.cutPhilosophy: Cuts are motivated by changed emotional ownership: Mum’s concern, Keen’s performance, the object’s meaning, the altered distance, the comic recovery, the new presence of Squeaky. Avoid automatic action-consequence-reaction coverage. The wristband moment may earn longer holds, but only while thought is changing inside the paws and faces. The wobble should not be over-explained; let one clear comic punctuation land, then move on to the dolphin’s surprise and the boat’s increasing distance.
treatments.openingImage: Mum’s paw rests near a boat rope she has not tied because it is already tied; beyond it Keen busies himself in the boat, trying to look ready before anyone has asked him to be.
treatments.closingImage: Keen, now wearing the vacant gold wristbands, nods earnestly to Squeaky beside the drifting boat while Mum stands on the dock behind him, small but warm, her laugh still wet on her face.
treatments.cinematographerChallenge: Challenge: do not turn this into safe farewell coverage with a dock two-shot and predictable over-shoulders. If Mum owns the experience, the camera must have the courage to privilege her withheld touch and let Keen sometimes be partially lost to movement, boat edge, or distance. The visual risk is necessary: the scene is about the cost of opening her hands, so the frame must feel the separation happen geometrically, not merely show people saying goodbye.

treatments.name: Treatment 2 — Keen Tries to Outrun the Lump in His Throat
treatments.audienceExperience: The audience rides with Keen’s performed confidence until the performance keeps snagging on real feeling. Children get the excitement of loading the boat, receiving important wristbands, wobbling into adventure, and meeting Squeaky. Adults recognize the borrowed phrases, the too-fast smile, and the child trying to make leaving easier for his mum by pretending it is easy for him.
treatments.emotionalPointOfView: Keen governs the emotional point of view. His want is to prove “I’ve got this” before anyone can see his paws disagree. His need is to let Mum’s promise enter him, not just use it as another brave line. Mum is seen through Keen’s awareness: at first as the person he reassures, then as the source of the words he borrows, then as the face he cannot quite keep looking at once the boat moves.
treatments.comicOrDramaticMechanism: The dramatic mechanism is borrowed confidence cracking under proximity to the real thing. Keen repeats the language of growing up as armour, but the wristbands make the armour too honest to perform with. The comic mechanism is anticipation to reversal: the scene promises a clean heroic departure, then the boat immediately makes him flap and recover by luck. The final dolphin exchange uses misunderstanding from Keen’s point of view: he wants so badly for the adventure to be underway that he accepts Squeaky’s chatter as if it is a proper introduction.
treatments.characterPerformanceStrategy: Keen is kinetic even when standing still: leaning toward the boat, checking the same bundle twice, nodding before Mum finishes, letting his head-tuft lead him into decisions. His eyes keep darting toward the water because the adventure is calling, then back to Mum because leaving hurts. His fear tell must be visible but modest here: a swallowed gulp at “big step,” paws tightening when the wristbands touch him, ears flattening just before he commits to push off. He squares himself because that is how he thinks courage looks. Mum’s performance is filtered through what Keen can bear to see: she smiles bravely for him, brushes his cheek with too much tenderness for him to answer in words, and laughs through the tear only once he has survived the wobble.
treatments.visualGrammar: The visual grammar is forward-leaning and threshold-driven. The camera often feels slightly ahead of Keen’s thoughts, drawn toward boat, water, rope, open horizon, then pulled back by Mum’s voice. Composition favours diagonals: dock planks leading out, boat nose turning away, ropes cutting between home and adventure. The warm morning is inviting but not weightless; brighter light sits on the boat and water, while the dock retains the soft density of home.
treatments.cameraCharacterRelationship: The camera acts like Keen’s courage before he has earned it: eager, curious, sometimes too quick to face the next thing. It discovers Mum’s emotional weight when Keen does — not by waiting safely on her reaction, but by being tugged back to her when his bravado catches. During the push-off, the camera is allowed to share boat instability, so the audience feels why “Still got it!” is a cover. Once Squeaky appears, the camera’s attention genuinely pivots with Keen into delighted curiosity.
treatments.movementVersusStillness: Keen supplies motion; Mum supplies gravity. Early movement is purposeful but a little excessive, as if doing enough tasks can prevent a quiet moment. The wristband reveal interrupts his momentum completely. That stop should feel like thought arriving in his body. After the promise, movement restarts, but changed: his push-off is brave because it follows the pause, not because it is smooth. The wobble is an honest body betraying the boast. Squeaky restores buoyancy without erasing the ache.
treatments.depthAndEnvironment: Depth is adventure pressure. The water is present from the start as a pull in Keen’s eyeline, but it expands only as he commits. The dock remains readable as home base; Mum, ropes, and pier posts form the protected near world. The boat gradually becomes its own moving pocket of space. Environmental reactions prove Keen’s state: the boat rocks harder than his confidence admits, the rope releases with a small finality, water ripples widen behind him. The vacant wristbands sit in shallow intimacy when given, then become part of Keen’s silhouette against open depth.
treatments.rhythmAndEscalation: The scene’s rhythm follows Keen’s breath: quick-bright at the start, a catch at “big step,” a held inhale around the wristbands, a soft exhale at “I love you,” then a flurry of action at push-off. Escalation is not louder emotion; it is the increasing impossibility of keeping the brave mask smooth. The comic wobble arrives exactly when the audience needs air. The Squeaky encounter turns the end from farewell into first adventure, carrying nervousness and excitement together.
treatments.cutPhilosophy: Cuts should feel like Keen’s attention changing, not like coverage obligation. Cut toward what he is using to stay brave — gear, water, Mum’s face, wristbands, boat edge — then cut away when he cannot hold the feeling. The wristbands deserve visual isolation because they change Keen’s state from no-cuffs to vacant cuffs. The departure can use continuity where wobble and recovery need to be felt as one bodily cause, but cut for comic punctuation if the cover-up lands stronger separated from the flail.
treatments.openingImage: Keen leans over the boat with too much purpose, one paw on a bundle and the other already reaching for the next task, while the open water glints past him like it has been waiting.
treatments.closingImage: Keen looks ahead from the drifting boat, nervous smile becoming real as Squeaky chatters beside him; the vacant wristbands catch ordinary morning light, not magic, while Mum’s dock is now behind him.
treatments.cinematographerChallenge: Challenge: resist making Keen’s confidence look competent. If the camera is too stable and admiring, it endorses the mask instead of revealing the gap beneath it. Let the lens be eager enough to get ahead, then embarrassed with him when the boat rocks. The scene needs physical instability and attention shifts, not heroic launch-page symmetry.

treatments.name: Treatment 3 — The Wristbands Measure the Distance Between Home and Cove
treatments.audienceExperience: The audience experiences the scene as a small ceremony that turns into a launch. The emotional centre is the vacant wristbands: children understand them as special family objects; adults feel the absent father and Mum’s courage in handing over what she has kept close. The scene should feel intimate without becoming hushed for too long, because Keen’s wobble and Squeaky’s splash keep grief inside play.
treatments.emotionalPointOfView: The governing point of view is the object’s meaning as shared by Mum and Keen. The wristbands are not magic yet and not a solution; they are memory made wearable. Mum’s want is to pass on protection. Keen’s want is to wear them as proof he is ready. Their shared need is to let the bands mean connection rather than pressure. The camera treats the empty gold as the silent third presence in the goodbye.
treatments.comicOrDramaticMechanism: The dramatic mechanism is inheritance becoming action: an object moves from Mum’s keeping to Keen’s paws, then from still memory to travelling promise. The comedy is status change through physical undercutting: the newly wristbanded, supposedly grown-up adventurer immediately becomes a flailing cub in a rocking boat, then appoints that accident as mastery with “Still got it!” Squeaky’s chatter reframes the ceremony into an adventure partnership before the ache can sit too heavily.
treatments.characterPerformanceStrategy: Mum handles the wristbands with ritual care but tries to make the moment sound ordinary enough for Keen to survive it. Her thumb may pause over the vacant settings before she offers them; the pause is thought, not decoration. Keen’s first reaction is stillness: the object lands before the meaning does. He should not instantly grin. He absorbs the weight, then chooses a real smile. When he slips them on, he tests the feel with a tiny turn of the cuffs — not a power-up, a grounding touch. Before leaving, he performs courage again, but the performance is now carrying something true. Squeaky’s arrival gives him permission to be curious instead of solemn.
treatments.visualGrammar: The visual grammar is circular and threshold-based: the round absence in the wristbands, Mum’s enclosing paws, the bowl-like boat, ripples spreading, the emotional circle of home opening into the wider water. The frames should repeatedly ask what holds Keen: Mum’s paws, the cuffs, the boat, then eventually the unseen promise. Light is warm and tactile on gold and fur; the vacant bezels remain visibly empty. No aquamarine crystal, no glow. Their power here is absence and touch.
treatments.cameraCharacterRelationship: The camera is not attached to a single face but to the transfer of meaning. It may begin with the ordinary objects of departure, then be pulled toward the wristbands when Mum reveals them, then travel with them into Keen’s paws and onto his body. After that, the camera’s allegiance shifts to the widening distance the wristbands now cross. It can abandon faces briefly for the object if the object is carrying the emotion, then return when behaviour changes. The camera discovers action from the level of paws, rope, boat rim, and waterline rather than administering the scene from a safe pier view.
treatments.movementVersusStillness: Stillness belongs to the wristbands. Around them, everything else wants to move: breeze through ropes, boat nudging, Keen’s restless packing, Mum’s almost-fidgets. When the bands appear, the scene settles into a quiet centre. Once they are on Keen, movement resumes with a new imbalance: the boat rocks, Keen’s limbs scramble, the cuffs flash as his paws grab for control. This makes the inherited object part of comedy as well as tenderness, keeping it alive rather than museum-like.
treatments.depthAndEnvironment: The pier environment is treated as a chain of circles and thresholds: coiled rope, dock posts, boat curve, ripples, horizon. Depth becomes meaningful when the wristbands leave Mum’s near space and travel into the open water on Keen. The father’s absence is carried by empty space inside the bands and by the slight openness between Mum and Keen after the promise. The environment should never overwhelm the exchange; it quietly confirms weight and leaving — rope slackens, boat separates, water fills the gap.
treatments.rhythmAndEscalation: The rhythm begins as everyday preparation, then tightens into ceremony when the wristbands are named. The father line creates the deepest quiet of the scene, but not the episode’s wordless nadir; it is a held breath, not a full stop. The promise completes the transfer. The push-off immediately tests the new grown-up identity in slapstick physics. Squeaky’s arrival turns the bands from goodbye object to travelling object: they are now part of Keen’s first connection beyond home.
treatments.cutPhilosophy: Cuts are motivated by the wristbands changing function: hidden keepsake, revealed inheritance, offered promise, worn grounding touch, visible proof on the departing cub. Avoid treating them as an insert by habit; only isolate them when the emotion has moved into them. Faces matter when thought changes because of the object. The boat wobble may cut away from the cuffs if the comedy belongs to the whole body, then return to them only if they remind us the laugh still carries ache.
treatments.openingImage: A coil of pier rope forms a loose circle beside Keen’s unpacked-and-repacked supplies; Mum’s paws enter holding another circle, the vacant wristbands still hidden against her.
treatments.closingImage: The boat glides away leaving widening ripples; Keen’s vacant wristbands are now small flashes of gold on the moving boat, with Squeaky’s fin breaking the water beside him and Mum anchored on the dock behind.
treatments.cinematographerChallenge: Challenge: do not photograph the wristbands as a generic precious prop. Their emptiness is the story, so the frame must let absence read: the vacant settings, the space between paws before release, the water opening after departure. If we default to faces-only sentiment, we lose the show’s central language of feeling made visible in the world. Let the object author the scene’s geometry.

treatmentSelection.selectedTreatment: Combined — Mum’s Hands Let Go Through the Empty Wristbands
combinedFrom: Treatment 1 — Mum’s Hands Let Go Before Her Heart Does
Treatment 3 — The Wristbands Measure the Distance Between Home and Cove
treatmentSelection.governingAudienceExperience: The audience should feel a parent-sized act of courage made visible through touch: children experience an exciting launch with special family wristbands, a wobble, and Squeaky’s invitation forward, while adults feel Mum opening her paws around love she cannot keep beside her.
treatmentSelection.rationale: Treatment 1 is the spine because it understands the scene’s truth: this goodbye is not mainly Keen leaving, but Mum letting him go without making her ache his burden. Its emotional point of view, restraint, interrupted touch, and widening geometry are exactly aligned with the episode’s heart relationship. Treatment 3 should be folded in as the scene’s visual grammar: the vacant wristbands must not be a generic precious prop or early magic object; their emptiness, weight, circles, and transfer from Mum’s keeping to Keen’s body make feeling visible in the show’s own language. The combined treatment gives the scene its strongest audience curve: practical packing, the breath-in of inheritance, the promise, the irreversible push-off, the comic wobble, then Squeaky turning goodbye into first adventure. It also protects the ache: the wristbands remain unlit, Mum remains behind, and the laugh does not erase the cost.
treatmentSelection.rejectionChecks: Treatment 2 is rejected as the governing approach because Keen’s POV makes the launch too eager and risks making the scene about a child’s performed bravery rather than the harder, truer question: can Mum let him go without letting him see what it costs her? It has useful details — Keen’s attention shifts, instability, and the mask cracking — but as the main treatment it would pull the scene toward adventure pressure before the goodbye has fully landed. Treatment 3 alone is not selected because an object-led ceremony could over-organize the emotion around the prop and soften the living relationship between Mum and Keen; it is strongest as visual authorship inside Mum’s POV. None of the selected material depends on fixed character lanes, keeping all characters visible, habitual action/reaction coverage, safe camera placement, repeated close-up punctuation, mechanical shot counts, generic ‘cinematic’ language, or merely illustrating the script. The selected combination explicitly rejects safe farewell coverage, permanent screen sides, faces-only sentiment, and automatic insert shots; the camera must discover separation through paws, rope, cuffs, boat instability, and widening water.

scene.location: Home pier and small boat at the edge of open water
scene.time: Warm morning, with a faint cooler pull beyond the dock
scene.purpose: Keen leaves home wearing his father’s vacant wristbands, while Mum makes the harder choice: opening her paws and letting her love travel farther than her arms. The scene plants the wristbands as memory, protection, and ache before the adventure begins.
scene.dramaticQuestion: Can Mum let Keen go without making her grief his burden, and can Keen receive her promise without hiding inside a brave performance?
scene.connectionFromPreviousScene: The episode has established forward energy and false bravado; this scene slows that energy into a real goodbye, turning Keen’s performed confidence into something more fragile and meaningful.
scene.handoverToNextScene: Keen leaves the dock with the vacant wristbands on, Squeaky beside him, and nervous excitement pulling him toward open water and the coming weather.

beats.sourceScript: Keen loads and re-checks the boat while his Mum watches with pride she is trying not to let spill into tears.
exactDialogue: KEEN'S MUM: Keen… are you sure you’ve got everything?
beats.whatChanges: The goodbye begins disguised as practical packing. Mum’s checking is really a delay; Keen’s busyness is really a performance of readiness.
beats.whoDrives: Keen's Mum drives the emotional change by asking a practical question whose weight is larger than the words.
beats.audienceAnticipation: Children anticipate the boat adventure starting; adults anticipate that Mum is asking because she is not ready to stop touching the moment.
beats.actionOrChoice: Mum’s paw hovers near an already-secure rope or bundle, then redirects into one more check. Keen re-checks something already packed and answers too brightly, using motion to avoid standing still under her gaze.
beats.consequence: Keen’s confidence is established as borrowed brightness rather than settled truth, while Mum’s restraint leaks through ordinary caretaking.
beats.emotionalOrComicHandover: The practical rhythm carries us into the first slowdown: Mum must name that this is not just packing, it is a big step.

beats.sourceScript: Mum admits the step is large; Keen looks out at the water, swallows, and answers with the line he has borrowed from her.
exactDialogue: KEEN'S MUM: I know… it’s just… this is a big step.
KEEN: Like you said… it’s part of growing up.
beats.whatChanges: The practical cover cracks. The scene moves from checking things to acknowledging the size of leaving.
beats.whoDrives: Keen's Mum drives by letting the true scale of the departure show; Keen responds by reaching for a grown-up phrase that steadies him only partly.
beats.audienceAnticipation: The audience anticipates whether Keen’s brave face will hold when the open water becomes visible as distance, not just adventure.
beats.actionOrChoice: Mum stops fussing long enough for the silence to expose her worry. Keen looks toward the water, swallows, then repeats the line she has given him as if saying it correctly might make him ready.
beats.consequence: Keen’s courage tell appears in miniature: the swallow precedes the brave answer. Mum sees both the effort and the child beneath it.
beats.emotionalOrComicHandover: The borrowed line creates room for the deeper inheritance: Mum reaches the point where words are not enough and the wristbands must enter.

beats.sourceScript: Mum reveals the worn vacant wristbands and names their meaning; Keen stills as the breeze moves through the pier ropes.
exactDialogue: KEEN'S MUM: Keen… it’s time for you to have your father’s wristbands.
KEEN'S MUM: I still feel him… every day.
beats.whatChanges: The scene becomes ceremonial without becoming formal: the father’s vacant wristbands turn the goodbye into inheritance.
beats.whoDrives: Keen's Mum drives, not by explaining the past, but by placing its weight into the present.
beats.audienceAnticipation: Children anticipate a special object being given; adults feel the breath-in of something kept close for a long time being surrendered.
beats.actionOrChoice: Mum reveals the worn gold wristbands carefully, as if even the air around them matters. Keen’s packing energy stops; his paws do not reach too fast. The pier ropes stir softly in the breeze during the father mention.
beats.consequence: The wristbands become visible as empty circles carrying memory rather than magic: unlit, vacant, and heavy with love. Keen’s performance pauses because he understands this is not an adventure accessory.
beats.emotionalOrComicHandover: The stillness hands into contact: the question is no longer what the wristbands mean, but whether Mum can physically let them go.

beats.sourceScript: Mum places the vacant wristbands into Keen's paws, asks for the promise, and he slips them on as she brushes his cheek.
exactDialogue: KEEN'S MUM: Promise me you’ll always wear them.
KEEN'S MUM: Wherever you go… You’ll never be alone.
beats.whatChanges: The wristbands pass from Mum’s keeping to Keen’s body. Love changes form from held-close to carried-away.
beats.whoDrives: Keen's Mum drives the transfer, but her hands reveal the cost; Keen’s stillness allows the promise to land before he performs again.
beats.audienceAnticipation: The audience anticipates whether Mum’s paws will open fully, and whether Keen will treat the gift as sacred rather than simply exciting.
beats.actionOrChoice: Mum places the vacant wristbands into Keen’s paws with controlled care, then asks for the promise before releasing the last contact. Keen receives them first with his paws, then with his face; he slips them on. Mum brushes his cheek, a touch that almost becomes holding on but stops itself.
beats.consequence: Keen is now in his vacant-wristbands state. The father’s absence is visible on his wrists, and Mum’s promise gives the empty bands emotional charge without lighting them or turning them into power.

shots.purpose: Open the scene as Mum’s delay disguised as caretaking.

shots.purpose: Show Keen performing readiness through needless motion.

shots.physicalPerformance: Keen reopens a packed bundle only far enough to prove he does not need to, tucks the same edge back down, and overcommits the finishing pat so the boat gives a faint answering bob. His chin lifts before his paws have fully stopped working.
shots.animationTiming: His line should jump in half a beat early, riding over the last fussy movement. The pat lands a touch too hard, then he freezes into satisfaction for just long enough to show he is performing readiness.

shots.purpose: Let the practical cover crack without melodrama.
shots.audienceExperience: The room feels the scene slow: this is no longer just packing.
shots.openingImage: Mum has no task left; her paws are still for the first time, with a thin strip of water visible beyond Keen’s boat.
shots.principalPerformance: She holds herself together through the line: “I know… it’s just… this is a big step.”

shots.physicalOrEmotionalChange: Mum names the size of leaving, and the dock becomes a threshold instead of a work space.
shots.closingImage: Her unfinished fussing hand settles against herself instead of reaching outward.

shots.physicalPerformance: With no object left to correct, Mum’s hands search for work and find only each other. A breath lifts her chest toward a sob; she swallows it into a controlled smile, and the hand that wanted to reach outward folds back against herself.
shots.animationTiming: Give the first stillness enough time to feel unfamiliar. Each ellipsis is a separate thought being managed: acceptance, the almost-break, then the practical shape she forces around the feeling.

shots.purpose: Make Keen’s borrowed bravery visible before he speaks it.
shots.audienceExperience: Children see him look toward adventure; adults catch the swallow before the brave phrase.
shots.openingImage: From inside the boat, the open water sits past Keen’s shoulder as distance rather than postcard space.
shots.principalPerformance: He looks out, swallows, then says carefully: “Like you said… it’s part of growing up.”
shots.cameraRelationship: Close with Keen, but the water is allowed to pull depth through the frame.
shots.physicalOrEmotionalChange: His courage tell appears: fear arrives first, then the grown-up line is borrowed to steady it.
shots.closingImage: His chin lifts after the line, a beat later than the words.
shots.transitionReason: Cut to the wristbands because words have reached their limit; remaining on Keen would pre-explain the inheritance with facial reaction before the object can carry its own weight.

shots.animationTiming: Hold the look to the water just long enough for the swallow to be unavoidable. The spoken phrase should steady across its length, with the chin lift delayed after the final word rather than landing with it.

shots.purpose: Introduce the wristbands as memory, not magic.

shots.openingImage: Mum’s careful paws reveal the worn vacant gold wristbands in compressed morning light.
shots.principalPerformance: Her hands treat the empty circles as precious and heavy while she says: “Keen… it’s time for you to have your father’s wristbands.”
shots.cameraRelationship: The camera gives the object temporary authority, with Mum present through touch rather than explanation.
shots.physicalOrEmotionalChange: The goodbye becomes inheritance; the father’s absence enters as visible emptiness.
shots.closingImage: The wristbands rest in Mum’s open paws, unlit, with pier ropes stirring softly behind.

shots.purpose: Show Keen’s performance stop before his face can manage a response.
shots.audienceExperience: A small breath-in: he understands this is not an adventure accessory.
shots.openingImage: Keen’s busy paws freeze over the packed bundle as the wristbands enter his awareness.
shots.principalPerformance: His hands do not reach too fast; his face is late to the seriousness his body has already understood.
shots.cameraRelationship: The camera abandons the object just enough to see its effect on Keen, not as automatic reaction but as changed meaning.
shots.physicalOrEmotionalChange: Keen’s readiness performance pauses; receiving replaces proving.
shots.closingImage: His paws lower, empty and waiting, with the boat’s movement suddenly quiet around him.

shots.animationTiming: Let the freeze register in the fingers before moving to the larger body. Keep the pause clean and brief: enough for understanding, not enough for worship.

shots.purpose: Make Mum’s courage visible as the opening of her paws.
shots.audienceExperience: Children watch the special gift pass to Keen; adults feel love changing form from held-close to carried-away.
shots.openingImage: Mum’s paws lower the vacant wristbands into Keen’s waiting paws; both sets of hands share the weight.

shots.physicalOrEmotionalChange: The wristbands pass from Mum’s keeping into Keen’s responsibility.
shots.closingImage: Mum’s last fingers lift away, leaving the wristbands fully in Keen’s paws.

shots.purpose: Let the promise move from object to body and cheek.
shots.audienceExperience: The audience feels the gift become something Keen carries, while Mum steals one final touch without holding on.
shots.openingImage: Keen slips the vacant wristbands onto his wrists; they remain unlit and ordinary-heavy.
shots.principalPerformance: Mum brushes his cheek and stops the touch before it becomes a grasp, saying: “Wherever you go… You’ll never be alone.”

shots.physicalOrEmotionalChange: The father’s absence becomes visible on Keen’s body, and Mum’s love is entrusted to distance.

shots.purpose: Land the emotional crest without sealing the ache away.

shots.physicalOrEmotionalChange: Keen accepts being held by love even as he leaves; Mum’s ache remains, not solved.
shots.closingImage: They share the closest stillness they can bear before the boat has to move.
shots.transitionReason: Cut to action because the crest has landed and staying would harden into sentiment; the scene needs the dock, boat, and water to take over before the ache becomes the whole ending.

shots.animationTiming: Give Keen’s first sentence a soft landing before the love line. Mum’s answer should breathe through the ellipsis, then end before the stillness turns into a tableau; protect the ache by leaving promptly.

shots.purpose: Turn goodbye into irreversible motion and release it through hiding failure.
shots.audienceExperience: Children get the launch wobble; adults get relief that the scene can laugh without erasing the cost.

shots.cameraRelationship: The camera commits to the unstable boat experience, not the safe dock view; it feels the wobble with him.
shots.physicalOrEmotionalChange: A widening strip of water opens between Mum and Keen, and Keen’s mask returns softer as comic cover-up.
shots.closingImage: Keen upright again by luck, chin lifted too fast, wristbands visible and unlit.

shots.physicalPerformance: Keen plants the push-off with more confidence than balance; the force travels through the pole or paw into the hull, and the boat rocks back under him. His knees chase the tilt, paws counterspin in widening circles, his weight overcorrects past center, and the boat’s recoil accidentally returns him upright; he snaps into a proud stance before his feet have fully believed it.
shots.animationTiming: Run the gag as one cause-chain: push, delayed hull answer, fast wobble, accidental catch. The boast comes a fraction too early, while the last wobble is still dying under him, making the cover-up the laugh.

shots.purpose: Let Mum’s wet laugh change the meaning of the wobble.

showrunnerJudgement: PASS. I tried to reject it on the usual Crystal Bears failure points — safe dock farewell coverage, automatic over-shoulders, glowing-object sentiment, wobble over-cutting, and Mum reduced to a reaction machine — but the scene keeps returning to the selected experience: a mother’s courage made visible through touch while the child’s adventure stays legible and funny. The wristbands remain vacant and heavy rather than magical; the boat wobble releases the ache without cancelling it; Squeaky changes the water from separation into invitation. The scene earns the breath-in and the laugh in the same passage.
treatmentComparison: Against “Mum’s Hands Let Go Before Her Heart Does,” this storyboard largely preserves the governing architecture. Mum owns the emotional point of view through hands, failed tasks, delayed release, and the wet laugh after Keen’s wobble. Keen’s performance begins over-bright, stops at the wristbands, returns softer as comic cover, then opens into curiosity with Squeaky. The visual grammar follows the treatment’s demand for hands, distance, and soft morning air: close rope/hand/object frames compress the farewell, then the water gains space after the handoff. The camera also answers the cinematographer challenge by not staying safely dock-bound: SH10 commits to the unstable boat experience before rediscovering Mum as the still point. The closing image matches the contract: Keen with vacant wristbands, Squeaky beside him, Mum behind him smaller but warm. The main risk is that the first four shots still flirt with alternating Mum/Keen line coverage, and several cards carry a lot of tiny performance notation, but these do not overturn the whole-scene experience because the cuts are tied to emotional ownership and the micro-behaviour is mostly load-bearing rather than decorative.
